subject: technology
lesson_title: Launch and diagnostic: what is an algorithm
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Algorithms and Programming
essential_question: How can understanding patterns, sequences, and introductory algorithms help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Activate prior knowledge about what is an algorithm, surface initial thinking without penalty, and establish the unit question.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of what is an algorithm.
Check, revise, or improve work about what is an algorithm using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about what is an algorithm.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
task_brief: This is day 1 of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". That is unit 4 in grade 3. Today is a diagnostic probe about what is an algorithm. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Write and test a step-by-step set of directions for a partner or character to follow. Today helps by working on what is an algorithm. Your unit also covers what is an algorithm, everyday sequences, giving step-by-step directions, and following a partner's directions. Today is for practice. You are scored on finishing and being honest, not on getting it perfect.
primary_task: First, write what you already think about what is an algorithm. Do this before anyone explains it. Draw or list the steps you think are needed. Then guess one thing that would break your steps. Try your steps on two examples you make up. Mark what worked. Mark what did not. A wrong guess is fine here. It does not lower your score. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about what is an algorithm. It is part of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". Later days in this unit cover other things, like everyday sequences. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about what is an algorithm; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, API key, or identifiable image.
Use only fictional or sandboxed systems, accounts, and data; never probe, exploit, or attempt to access a real external system.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify, not as an authority or a substitute for learner work.
The tutor may explain, demonstrate, or debug alongside the learner, but must not silently complete a graded project or assessment for them.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting what is an algorithm.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for what is an algorithm follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for what is an algorithm, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for what is an algorithm works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of what is an algorithm, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking what is an algorithm mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply what is an algorithm under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on what is an algorithm rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
